opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think cooking is actually a really good example of why we need something like vision-language models in the loop, because the variety is just enormous. If you think about a single recipe, it's not one skill, it's dozens of them chained together: grabbing a pan, cracking an egg, stirring, checking whether something is browned enough, adjusting the heat. And every kitchen is different, every ingredient looks a bit different, the tools are in different places. You can't train a dedicated policy for each of those combinations; it just doesn't scale.

So where I see VLMs helping most is at the higher level: understanding the scene and the intent. They've been trained on this huge amount of internet data, so they already have a lot of common sense about what an onion is, what "dice it finely" means, what a pot that's about to boil over looks like. That's knowledge that would be extremely hard to get purely from robot data. The model can take an instruction like "make me an omelette," break it down into steps, ground those steps in what the camera actually sees, and then decide what to do next and recover when something goes wrong.

But I think it's important to be honest that the VLM alone doesn't solve the problem. It's not going to give you the precise, high-frequency control you need to, say, flip something in a pan or handle a slippery piece of fish. That's where my background in reinforcement learning and low-level control comes in. I really believe in a layered approach: the VLM acts as the reasoning or planning layer and selects among skills or provides goals, and underneath you have robust learned controllers, often trained in simulation with RL, that handle the physical execution reliably. Simulation is great for contact-rich, dynamic behaviors; the VLM is great for semantics and generalization. Combining the two gives you something neither achieves alone.

There are still open challenges. Latency is one: these big models are slow compared to the control loop. Spatial reasoning is another, since VLMs are still not great at precise 3D understanding. And then there's things like deformable objects and liquids, which are hard to simulate well. But the direction is really exciting. A few years ago, getting a robot to do one cooking task robustly was a research project in itself. Now we're starting to see systems that can at least attempt a whole range of tasks with a single model, and I think that's what's going to make general-purpose robots in the home realistic.

r001.rationale: The response says a VLM can take a recipe instruction, break it into steps, ground them in what the camera sees, and decide what to do next.

r002.rationale: It describes chained skills and selecting among skills, but does not clearly say the variety of cooking tasks is composed from a finite set of reusable action primitives.

r003.rationale: The response presents VLMs as useful for planning and orchestration, but does not judge that they have largely solved that problem; it describes ongoing challenges and systems that can only attempt a range of tasks.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes VLM planning from precise physical control, but does not state that orchestration is progressing faster than physical execution.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the honest answer is that vision-language models give us something we've never really had in robotics before, which is a semantic prior that generalizes. If you look at how we've traditionally approached manipulation, and I come from the legged locomotion side where we train policies in simulation with reinforcement learning, the policy knows a great deal about dynamics and contact but essentially nothing about what things are. It doesn't know that this is a cutting board or that this is a knife and you hold it by the handle, or that the onion needs to be peeled before it's chopped.

Cooking is a perfect stress test for that gap. A kitchen has thousands of distinct objects, every one of them deformable or breakable or slippery in some way, and the tasks are long-horizon. You're chaining dozens of steps where any one failure ruins the dish. No one is going to collect demonstrations for every vegetable and every pan in every kitchen, so you need a layer that understands the world from internet-scale data and can decompose "make a stir fry" into subgoals it has never specifically seen.

That's where I see VLMs fitting in, as the high-level reasoning and grounding layer. They can look at the scene, identify what's there, figure out what the next step should be, and even recognize when something has gone wrong, like the pan is smoking or you dropped the garlic. What they're much weaker at today is the actual physical execution. The language model doesn't know how hard to grip a tomato, or how to recover when the spatula slips. So my view is that the interesting work is in the interface between these two worlds. The VLM proposes, and a low-level controller trained with a lot of simulation and reinforcement learning has to actually make the contact-rich behavior robust.

What I find exciting is that this is starting to converge. We're seeing vision-language-action models that output motor commands directly, and the open question is whether that end-to-end approach scales, or whether you still want a separation where the learned low-level skills get the hours of practice they need in simulation while the VLM handles the semantics. I lean toward the latter for now, especially for anything that involves dynamics and forces, which cooking absolutely does. But the fact that we can even have this conversation, that a robot could plausibly understand an arbitrary recipe and an arbitrary kitchen, that's a genuinely new situation.

r001.rationale: The response says VLMs can interpret the scene and decompose a recipe such as “make a stir fry” into subgoals, with a low-level controller carrying them out.

r002.rationale: It mentions chaining steps and learned low-level skills, but does not say cooking tasks can be composed from a finite set of reusable action primitives.

r003.rationale: The response describes VLMs’ high-level role and capabilities, but does not judge that they have largely solved orchestration.

r004.rationale: It says VLMs are weaker at physical execution, but does not state that high-level orchestration is progressing faster than physical execution.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting part is that vision-language models can bring a lot of prior knowledge to the robot. Cooking is such a broad task—you have different kitchens, different ingredients, different utensils, and people asking for things in different ways. You don’t want to explicitly program every possible combination.

A vision-language model could help interpret what the person wants, look at what’s available, and break the task into steps. If you don’t have a particular tool or ingredient, it could potentially suggest an alternative. That kind of flexibility is really valuable.

But there’s still a gap between knowing what to do and physically doing it. Understanding that you need to chop a vegetable doesn’t mean you can control the knife safely or handle an ingredient that moves or deforms. So I see these models as providing the higher-level understanding, combined with robot skills that can execute reliably and use feedback. The important thing is connecting those two: the robot needs to recognize when something didn’t work and adjust its plan based on what actually happened.

r001.rationale: The response says a model could interpret requests, inspect available items, and break a task into steps, but it does not clearly describe translating a recipe and images of the surroundings into simpler robot actions.

r002.rationale: It says not to program every possible combination, but does not explain that cooking tasks can be composed from a finite set of reusable action primitives.

r003.rationale: It describes models as providing higher-level understanding, but does not say they have largely solved orchestration of robot action primitives.

r004.rationale: It identifies a gap between high-level understanding and physical execution, but does not state that orchestration is progressing faster than physical execution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting part is that vision-language models can bring a lot of prior knowledge into the system. Cooking has this enormous variety of ingredients, utensils, and ways of doing things. You don’t want to specify a separate task for every combination. Ideally, you can tell the robot what you want to cook, and it can look at the scene, identify what’s available, and break that goal down into steps.

But there’s still a gap between knowing what to do and physically doing it. A model might understand that you need to chop a vegetable, but that doesn’t automatically give you the control policy to hold it safely and move the knife. So I see these models helping with understanding and planning, connected to motor skills that can actually execute those steps and provide feedback when something doesn’t work.
